patch.why: Predictive design has two routes. (1) A validated transport closure (plasma-hall-anomalous-closure), first-principles or data-driven, inside cheap fluid or hybrid codes, or surrogates trained on many kinetic runs, which amounts to the same thing. (2) From 2033 in S3 and 2034 in S2, direct optimization on full-device kinetic runs (plasma-35-kinetic-design-loop). Before then, whole-device kinetic simulation only supplies training and validation data: at days per run on a leadership-class machine it cannot serve the hundreds of evaluations a design loop needs (arithmetic in plasma-kinetic-solvers-at-scale). Either route is enough, so both are soft edges; the years (S3 2029, S2 2030, S1 2035) come from the closure route. A new Hall thruster typically takes several build-test iterations at roughly a year each (general); a predictive code could cut iterations from ~3-4 to ~1-2 (general, judgment). Validation needs test data across designs, which binds the year. The band follows the closure: S2 Low and S3 Medium by 2031. The two routes share wall and emission physics and the need for test data, so together they do not lift the band to High by 2035.

patch.why: A 23,000-hour wear test is 2.6 years of continuous firing. Running ~10,000 hours and extrapolating with an accepted model would save ~1.5 years and tens of millions in facility time (general). The step beyond today's practice is predicting how erosion evolves as surfaces wear, beyond the tested duration. That needs a near-wall transport model that stays valid as geometry changes (plasma-hall-anomalous-closure, hard) and a rule for crediting model evidence (physclock-credibility-evidence-standard, hard). Design-before-build (plasma-ep-predictive-design) and certification of AI-written proofs (infra-tool-qualification, which covers software proof credit, not physics wear models) help but are not required. Chain (S3): closure validated 2029 -> a wear test planned for partial credit accumulates ~10,000 h (about 16 months at a normal wear-test duty cycle), checked against long-duration data (AEPS QM-2 completes Sep 2029) -> qualification review -> 2031 at the earliest. S2 lands at the horizon, one step later. Full-device kinetic runs (plasma-35-kinetic-design-loop, soft, S3 2033) can resolve near-wall erosion later, but low-energy sputter yields and agency practice still bind. The regulator rule caps the band at Medium. After compounding it is Low in all scenarios at both checkpoints.

patch.description: Development-to-qualification time for new EP thrusters falls ~15-30% (S2), up to ~40% (S3), and build-test iterations roughly halve because physics-based models replace parts of empirical iteration and, where an agency accepts it, of wear testing. patch.why: Predictive design (fewer iterations) is enough for commercial thrusters, where no certifier sits above the operator: cutting 1.5-2 years from a 4-6 year program is 25-40%, which meets the S2 threshold (plasma-ep-predictive-design). Model-based life credit (plasma-ep-life-by-analysis, soft) would shorten agency wear tests further, but it is Low by 2035, so it is off the critical path. The outcome needs at least one full development-to-qualification cycle started after predictive design is validated, still with a full wear test. Chain (S3): predictive design 2029 -> program started 2030 -> design, one or two build-test iterations and a full wear test in about three years -> 2033. S2: predictive design 2030 -> 2034. S1: predictive design 2035 -> after 2035. Band Low in S2-S4: predictive design is Medium by 2035, and the cut must be shown on a real program and published.

add_nodes.title: Whole-thruster kinetic runs fast enough for design loops
add_nodes.description: Full-device 3D kinetic simulation of a 5 kW-class Hall thruster at real mass ratio, with neutrals and wall emission, runs in hours on a leadership-class machine or in about a day on a commercial cluster. A design loop can then afford hundreds of kinetic evaluations, so thruster design no longer has to wait for a universal transport closure.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: No facility-scale kinetic simulation of a Hall thruster exists at feasible cost (Whittaker, Marks, Gorodetsky, AIAA 2026). The tree's estimate for a 1 ms full-device run is about 1e18-1e19 particle pushes, weeks to months on a full exascale machine today (plasma-kinetic-solvers-at-scale).
add_nodes.why: Days per run (plasma-kinetic-solvers-at-scale, S2 2028) still rules out design loops. Hours per run needs another 10-50x. The parent already uses the main algorithm families (sparse-grid, low-rank, asymptotic-preserving, learned subgrid models) to reach days, so a second 3-10x from them is the optimistic case and needs S3's recursive algorithm work from 2029. Hardware for memory-bound particle-in-cell codes gains about 3-5x over 2028-33 (judgment). Large AI clusters add capacity, but by 2028 leadership-class machines are built from the same accelerators (general), so they do not add a separate factor. Chain (S3): hero runs 2028 -> four years of recursive algorithm work and newer hardware -> design-loop speed 2033. S2: 2034. S1 does not get there by 2035. With hours-long runs, designers can optimize on kinetic physics directly and use the closure (plasma-hall-anomalous-closure) as a check. Medium in S3 because gains may stall and surrogates may make the full loop unnecessary. Algorithms and compute bind, so S4 equals S3.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Some cost may be irreducible: electron-cyclotron drift waves must be resolved over a millisecond of xenon transit, and algorithm gains could stall near 10x. Surrogates trained on a few hero runs may give designers the same answer more cheaply.
add_nodes.signpost: A paper or company reports a design optimization that ran at least 100 full-device kinetic simulations of a Hall thruster, each at real mass ratio and real geometry.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: the step after hero runs, 2033 in S3 and 2034 in S2. It gives predictive design a second route that does not wait for a universal transport closure, and gives the closure and erosion models many more training cases. Algorithms and compute bind, so S4 equals S3.

Advocate's hardware point partly accepted (3-5x for memory-bound PIC; AI clusters are not a separate factor once leadership machines use the same accelerators); its S2 2033, S2 Medium and S3 High rejected. Skeptic's S2 2035 and S3 Low rejected. Soft edges added to plasma-ep-predictive-design, plasma-hall-anomalous-closure and plasma-ep-life-by-analysis (advocate).

add_nodes.title: AI-designed thrusters fly across a whole constellation
add_nodes.description: An electric thruster designed mainly by an AI optimization loop (as defined in plasma-ai-designed-thruster-flight) flies on at least 1,000 satellites of one constellation, with fleet performance inside the pre-flight predicted band and the design attribution public.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Starlink flies thousands of Hall thrusters (krypton, then argon) designed by conventional iteration (general). No AI-designed thruster has flown (plasma-ai-designed-thruster-flight).
add_nodes.why: Constellation operators refresh satellite generations about yearly from 2029-31 (physclock-satellite-gen-cadence) and build thrusters in house, so a design that proves itself in one flight can enter the next generation. Chain (S2): first AI-designed thruster flight 2031 -> adopted in the next satellite generation 2032 -> 1,000 units flown 2033. S3: 2032. S1: first flight 2033 -> 2035, at the horizon, so Speculative. The band is held down by disclosure, because operators may not say how a thruster was designed. Satellite generations and launch set the pace, and thruster production is not the bottleneck, so S4 equals S3.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Constellation thrusters are cheap and mature, and their economics turn on propellant, power-processing mass and production rate. A few points of efficiency may not justify changing a working design, and an in-house design loop may never be described in public.
add_nodes.signpost: A constellation operator states that a new satellite generation flies a thruster designed mainly by an AI loop, with fleet performance data.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: fleet adoption after the first flight, 2032 in S3 and 2033 in S2. Satellite generations and launch set the pace, so S4 equals S3.

add_nodes.title: Air-breathing electric propulsion in operational service
add_nodes.description: At least one operational satellite (commercial or government; technology demonstrations do not count) holds a mission orbit below 250 km for at least a year, using air-breathing electric propulsion for drag makeup.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Laboratory demonstrations only (general). Albedo's Clarity-1 flew at 350-380 km on xenon ion propulsion for nine months (Albedo, Jan 2026). No air-breathing thruster has flown (plasma-abep-demo).
add_nodes.why: A demo (S2 2031, S3 2030) proves intake and discharge physics. An operational unit also needs endurance data, a product design and a customer who values orbits below 250 km, where stored propellant runs out. Chain (S3): demo 2030 -> one to two years of on-orbit endurance, including atomic-oxygen erosion, and a funded product -> first operational satellite 2033 -> a year in service 2034. S2: 2035. S1: demo 2033 -> after 2035. An operational unit must also be sized for the solar cycle 26 maximum, expected around 2035 (general), when density at 200-250 km is several times higher; a demo near the 2030-31 minimum does not test that. Low at best because the business case competes with conventional electric propulsion at 300-380 km and with cheap replacement launches. Launch, customers and endurance data bind, so S4 equals S3.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Cheap launch makes short-lived low-orbit satellites easy to replace, and conventional electric propulsion already holds 300-380 km. Intake efficiency and atomic-oxygen erosion may keep air-breathing propulsion a niche.
add_nodes.signpost: A low-orbit operator orders an air-breathing propulsion system for an operational satellite, or an in-orbit demo reports more than six months of drag makeup.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: service after the first demo, 2034 in S3 and 2035 in S2. Launch, customers and endurance data bind, so S4 equals S3.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-plasma-nuclear (2026-10-07): new node for the 2035 horizon; extends plasma-abep-demo to operational service. | Resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic accepted: S3/S4 2033 -> 2034, S2 2034 -> 2035, band_2035 S2 Low -> Speculative (zero slack); solar-cycle sizing added to why.

add_nodes.title: A reactor-powered electric spacecraft thrusts for a year
add_nodes.description: A spacecraft powered by a space fission reactor (Space Reactor-1 Freedom or a successor) runs its electric thrusters on reactor power for a cumulative year in space. These are the first nuclear-electric propulsion operations.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: SR-1 Freedom (over 20 kWe, HALEU fuel, Gateway PPE bus with three 12 kW AEPS and four 6 kW Hall thrusters) targets a Dec 2028 launch at a $2.1B estimate (Sep 2026), with $10M recommended by the House Appropriations Committee (May 2026). No U.S. reactor has flown since SNAP-10A (1965).
add_nodes.why: SR-1 must launch toward Mars in a Mars window. At about 20 kWe its thrust is about 1 N or less, roughly 1e-4 m/s2 on a several-tonne craft, so spiralling out from low orbit would take about two years (general arithmetic). A launch in the early-2031 window, the earliest year of physclock-reactor-in-space in every scenario, gives a cumulative year of thrust in 2032, and only if FY2027 or FY2028 funds SR-1 in full. The next window, about Apr 2033, gives 2034. A mid-2035 launch finishes after 2035. A lunar reactor does no thrusting. The AEPS thrusters on the PPE bus finish their wear test in Sep 2029 (plasma-aeps-life-qual), so thruster life is not the gate. Low in every scenario because the reactor launch is Low by 2035 and only the 2031 and 2033 windows count. Appropriations and launch windows bind, so S4 equals S3.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Every U.S. space reactor program since 1965 has been cancelled, and SR-1 is underfunded against its Dec 2028 date. If SR-1 misses the Apr 2033 window, a year of nuclear-electric thrust waits past 2035.
add_nodes.signpost: SR-1 Freedom receives a full FY2027 or FY2028 appropriation and a firm launch date; a ground criticality test of its reactor.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: the propulsion payoff of SR-1, 2032 at the earliest in every scenario. Only the early-2031 and Apr 2033 Mars windows give a full year of thrust by 2035. Appropriations and launch windows bind, so S4 equals S3.

S1 2033 -> 2032; the skeptic's 2034 is rejected because physclock-reactor-in-space now has the early-2031 window as its earliest year in every scenario. Advocate's S2-S4 Medium rejected: it rested on a Medium reactor band, now Low.

add_nodes.title: A fusion-drive prototype makes fusion and thrust on the ground
add_nodes.description: A ground prototype built to a closed fusion-propulsion design (plasma-fusion-propulsion-design-closure), using the magnet, heating and nozzle layout of that design at no less than one-tenth of its design heating power, produces measured fusion reactions while exhausting plasma through its magnetic nozzle, with thrust measured. Breakeven is not required. A fusor, or a device without a nozzle, does not count.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Direct Fusion Drive is a concept tested at small scale at PPPL (PFRC). Pulsar Fusion's Sunbird exhaust (no fusion) is targeted for an in-orbit demonstration in 2027 (pulsarfusion.com). No fusion-propulsion prototype has produced fusion.
add_nodes.why: Chain (S3): design closure 2030 -> funding 2031 -> 4-6 years to build and commission a new device, as for SPARC (about six years from construction to its 2027 first-plasma target, after slips) and Helion's Polaris (about four to five years with large private funding; general) -> 2035 at the earliest. S2: closure 2031 -> after 2035. S1: closure 2034 -> after 2035. Deuterium fuel is enough to show fusion products, so He-3 supply does not gate this step. Speculative because fusion-propulsion funding is small and compact field-reversed devices have not reached fusion-relevant conditions. Funding runs on investor and appropriations clocks that do not differ by scenario, and experiments bind, so S4 equals S3.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Fusion-propulsion firms are small and thinly funded, and a flight-like mass budget is far harder than a lab device. A credible design does not by itself bring the money to build one.
add_nodes.signpost: NASA, DARPA, ESA or private investors fund a fusion-propulsion prototype build; a PFRC-class experiment reports deuterium fusion neutrons.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: the ground step between a closed design and flight, 2035 at the earliest in S3 and after 2035 in S2. Building a new fusion device takes 4-6 years after funding in every scenario, so it is Speculative. Experiments and funding bind, so S4 equals S3.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-plasma-nuclear (2026-10-07): new node for the 2035 horizon; extends the fusion-propulsion chain between design closure and flight; spine. | Resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic accepted in full: S3/S4 2034 -> 2035, S2 2035 -> >2035, band_2035 S3/S4 Low -> Speculative; description made checkable (one-tenth of the design's heating power with its magnet, heating and nozzle layout, replacing 'flight-like mass per unit of power', which has no meaning below breakeven). Both reviewers: the link to plasma-fusion-propulsion-flight is now a hard edge.
